extracted.intended_audience: historians of science, scholarly publishing researchers, and academic readers interested in the history and functions of peer review
extracted.subtask_description: A short historical account of the roles and functions that early peer review (especially at the Royal Society and in nineteenth-century learned societies) performed, and how those functions differed from the modern association of peer review with quality control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accrediting ‘proper’ research and researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Refereeing is widely believed to add significant value as a means of accrediting ‘proper’ research and researchers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although refereeing delays publication, it is commonly understood (in contemporary discourse) to confer accreditation and legitimacy on both individual researchers and their work. The essay situates this belief as part of a later-history interpretation rather than an immutable function from the origins of journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing as quality control (modern association)
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern association between refereeing and ‘quality control’ did not emerge until the mid-twentieth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating peer review primarily as a mechanism of quality control is anachronistic for earlier periods: the function of refereeing shifted over time, and only in the mid-1900s did quality-control become the dominant framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective editorial responsibility to reduce reputational and financial risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective editorial responsibility was a way of reducing the reputational and financial risk of poor decisions for the Society as a corporate body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practices created an impression of collective decision-making by a community of scholars, thereby distributing accountability and protecting institutional reputation and finances. This social/organizational function was central in earlier editorial systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees as stewards of the Society’s finances (intellectual-justification gatekeeping)
rubrics_metrics.description: By the beginning of the twentieth century, referees were specifically tasked to decide whether there was sufficient intellectual justification for so many pages and illustrations — acting as stewards of the Society’s finances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was a cost-control function: referees assessed the justificatory value of submissions relative to publication costs. The essay also notes the historical critique that referees were 'not actually very good at' this task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking for logical flaws and factual errors
rubrics_metrics.description: In the nineteenth century referees pointed out logical flaws or errors of fact in submitted manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This epistemic-checking function focused on identifying clear mistakes rather than proposing extensive revisions. It represents one concrete substantive duty referees performed in earlier eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring adequate acknowledgement of prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees were likely to comment on inadequate acknowledgement of the work of previous scholars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcing norms of citation and attribution was a prominent refereeing activity, aimed at maintaining scholarly propriety and the perceived integrity of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication as a badge of prestige and reward-system currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Successfully navigating editorial processes became a badge of prestige for authors; publication in learned society journals carried significant weight in reward and recognition systems of early twentieth-century British academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication functioned as social capital and career currency. The essay emphasizes that contemporary academic incentives and prestige systems are part of this historical legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing as gatekeeping rather than substantive revision
rubrics_metrics.description: The nineteenth-century refereeing process did not usually suggest significant revisions to manuscripts; its role was more gatekeeping within a complex editorial system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with many modern practices where referees often request substantive revisions. Historically, referees more commonly decided acceptance/rejection or flagged errors, rather than iteratively shaping manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergence of written refereeing practice (1830s)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society began using written refereeing in the 1830s (with similar practices emerging in other learned societies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This marks the procedural emergence of a practice resembling modern peer review; the timing matters for understanding when particular functions and expectations developed.
